title: How do you calculate break-even volume in one line?
description: Break-even in one line: a quick way to do this case calculation in your head, with a worked example.
hook: Break-even volume is fixed costs divided by contribution per unit, where contribution is price minus variable cost per unit. That one line answers "how many do we need to sell to cover our costs?", which is one of the most common calculations in a case.
body:
The one-line formula

Fixed costs are $400k. The price is $80 and the variable cost is $60 a unit. What is break-even volume?

Break-even volume = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit)

  1. Contribution per unit: $80 − $60 = $20.
  2. Break-even: $400,000 ÷ $20 = 20,000 units.
  3. Check: 20,000 × $20 = $400,000, exactly the fixed costs.

The logic: every unit sold chips $20 off the fixed costs. Once enough units have covered them, each further unit is profit. The contribution margin is the number that drives everything.

How to say it in the interview

"Break-even is fixed costs over contribution per unit. Contribution is $80 minus $60, so $20. $400k over $20 is 20,000 units. The question now is whether the client can realistically sell 20,000 units: what's the size of the market?"

The last sentence matters most. A break-even number is only useful when you compare it with something: market size, current sales, capacity or the client's time frame.

Ask what happens after break-even

Above 20,000 units, each sale adds $20 of profit. At 25,000 units, profit is (25,000 × $20) − $400,000 = $100,000, provided the client can make and sell that many at the same price and cost.

Test the price sensitivity

Break-even is very sensitive to price, because a price cut comes straight out of contribution. If the price falls to $75 while variable cost stays at $60, contribution falls to $15 and break-even rises to $400,000 ÷ $15 = 26,666.7, which rounds up to 26,667 units.

A 6% price cut has raised the volume needed by a third. That is the insight to say out loud in a pricing case.

Three useful variations

Break-even revenue

Multiply units by price, or divide fixed costs by the contribution margin as a percentage. At $80, contribution is 25% of price, so $400k ÷ 0.25 = $1.6M. At $75, it is 20%, so $400k ÷ 0.20 = $2.0M. Do not confuse break-even units with break-even revenue: when price changes, they move by different amounts.

Volume for a target profit

Add the target to the fixed costs: (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution. To make $100k at $80, the client needs ($400k + $100k) ÷ $20 = 25,000 units.

Break-even market share

Divide break-even volume by the market size. If the market is 200,000 units a year, 20,000 units means a 10% share. Whether 10% is easy or heroic depends on who else is competing.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing by price instead of contribution. $400k ÷ $80 = 5,000 units ignores the variable cost and badly understates the volume needed.
  • Including variable costs in "fixed costs". Ask which costs change with volume before you start. Fixed and variable costs covers how to split them.
  • Rounding down. 26,666.7 units means 26,667, because 26,666 still leaves a small loss.
  • Stopping at the number without comparing it with the market or the client's sales.

Practice

1. Fixed costs are $2.4M, price is $40 and variable cost is $25. What is break-even volume?

Show the answer

Contribution is $40 − $25 = $15. $2.4M ÷ $15 = 160,000 units.

2. Same business: how many units does it need to make $600k profit?

Show the answer

($2.4M + $0.6M) ÷ $15 = $3M ÷ $15 = 200,000 units.

3. If the market is 1M units a year, what share does break-even require?

Show the answer

160,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 16%. For a new entrant, that is a big ask in year one, so the next question is how quickly it could get there.
